strengths: Compelling motivation: The paper identifies a clear limitation in standard agentic RAG systems—namely treating retrieval as a black-box text querying interface—and proposes a Corpus Interaction Engine that exposes fine-grained retrieval actions (multi-faceted dense/sparse fusion, entity anchoring, and context shaping).

Cohesive system design: The methodology effectively combines a hierarchical reasoning workflow (Global-Planner, Adaptive-Reasoner, Executor) for trajectory synthesis/zero-shot execution with an end-to-end training pipeline utilizing SFT followed by RL (GRPO).
Strong empirical performance: The proposed Interact-RAG achieves consistent and significant gains over competitive baselines across six diverse single-hop and multi-hop QA benchmarks.

Thorough analysis and ablations: The authors provide detailed ablation experiments dissecting the contributions of the interaction engine, SFT, RL, and hierarchical workflow, alongside informative analyses of retrieval efficiency and interaction frequencies across training stages.
weaknesses: Corpus simplification and benchmark setup: As described in Appendix C.3, the evaluation corpus is downscaled/filtered to ~280,000 chunks based on benchmark metadata and ground-truth retrieval, rather than the full ~21 million passages standard Wikipedia corpus. This considerably reduces distractor complexity, and it remains somewhat unclear how cleanly official baseline checkpoints (e.g., Search-R1 trained for open retrieval) translate to this condensed corpus.

Backbone fairness in Table 1: In the primary results table (Table 1), Interact-RAG is built on Qwen3-8B while competitive trained baselines (Search-R1, R-Search, S-DeepSearcher) use official Qwen2.5-7B checkpoints. Although Table 4 provides Qwen2.5-7B comparisons, in Table 4 Search-R1 actually outperforms Interact-RAG on Natural Questions (45.3 vs 43.7 EM), which should be highlighted more directly in the main text.

Computational cost and latency analysis: The proposed interactive engine involves multi-turn interactions, hybrid score normalization, and filtering. The paper lacks a concrete evaluation of inference latency, wall-clock retrieval time, and total token overhead compared to standard iterative RAG baselines.

strengths: Compelling motivation: The paper identifies a clear and practical limitation of prevailing agentic RAG systems—namely, treating retrieval as an opaque black box that restricts agents to repetitive query paraphrasing when faced with retrieval failure.

Well-structured framework: The proposed Corpus Interaction Engine provides intuitive, fine-grained action primitives (multi-faceted dense/sparse fusion, entity-anchored matching, and context shaping). The progression from a modular reasoning workflow to synthetic trajectory generation, SFT, and GRPO reinforcement learning is sound and coherent.

Extensive experimental evaluation: The approach is evaluated across six standard QA benchmarks (covering single-hop and multi-hop scenarios) and demonstrates strong performance gains over static, iterative, and agentic baselines.

Insightful analysis: The paper includes meaningful analyses beyond final accuracy, such as retrieval efficiency (fewer interaction iterations), RL optimization dynamics, and an examination of how action primitive usage evolves across training stages.
weaknesses: Unfair baseline comparison in the main results (Table 1): The main table compares the proposed method running on Qwen3-8B against several key open-source baselines (Search-R1, R-Search, S-DeepSearcher) running on Qwen2.5-7B checkpoints. While the authors include a Qwen2.5-7B evaluation in Appendix Table 4, the headline claim of a 22.5% relative improvement in the main text is inflated by this backbone discrepancy. When compared strictly on Qwen2.5-7B (Table 4), the average EM gain over Search-R1 is 10.1%, and Search-R1 actually outperforms Interact-RAG on NQ (45.3 vs. 43.7).

Non-standard downsampled corpus: According to Appendix C.3, the evaluation corpus is downsampled to ~280,000 chunks constructed using dataset metadata and question-answer synthetic retrieval, rather than evaluating on the full multi-million-passage Wikipedia corpus commonly used in open-domain QA. It should be clarified whether baseline checkpoints were re-evaluated on this exact filtered subset and whether this curated setting artificially inflates entity-match effectiveness.

Lack of latency and compute cost profiling: While the paper shows Interact-RAG requires fewer interaction turns (Figure 3), each turn executes richer actions (hybrid search, entity filtering, reasoning traces). A thorough breakdown of inference latency, token usage, and database query overhead compared to standard query-only agents is missing.

Moderate conceptual novelty of retrieval primitives: The primitives (dense/BM25 score interpolation, SQLite FTS entity matching, chunk include/exclude filters) are standard information retrieval tools; the primary technical contribution lies in framing and training them within an agentic tool-use and RL policy rather than in novel retrieval mechanics.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated bottleneck in agentic RAG: moving beyond single semantic query reformulation loops by giving agents explicit control over retrieval strategies (hybrid search, entity filtering, context shaping).

Presents a complete end-to-end framework: utilizes a modular planning-reasoning-executing workflow to synthesize clean trajectories for SFT, followed by GRPO reinforcement learning to internalize strategic decision-making.
Provides interesting behavioral analyses, such as tracking how action frequency (e.g., entity matching vs. document shaping) shifts across training stages (non-trained vs. SFT vs. RL).
Evaluates on a wide variety of both multi-hop and single-hop question-answering benchmarks.
weaknesses: Severe evaluation protocol issues and potential test contamination: The paper deviates from standard open-domain retrieval benchmarks (which typically use the full ~21M passage Wikipedia dump) by constructing a downsampled ~280,000 chunk corpus. Crucially, for datasets lacking candidate passage metadata (e.g., Bamboogle), the corpus was populated by querying using both the question and the ground-truth answer. This introduces artificial data leakage and drastically simplifies the retrieval task compared to standard settings.

Unfair baseline comparisons in the main results (Table 1): The proposed method uses a newer Qwen3-8B backbone while the strongest RL/SFT baselines (Search-R1, R-Search, S-DeepSearcher) use older Qwen2.5-7B checkpoints. Although Qwen2.5-7B ablation results are placed in Appendix B.1, the gap narrows considerably (47.5 vs 43.1 EM), and evaluating off-the-shelf models trained on open-web/full-Wikipedia on a custom 280k corpus heavily disadvantages the baselines.

Limited algorithmic novelty: The 'Corpus Interaction Engine' essentially exposes standard search parameters (BM25 keyword search via SQLite FTS, dense embedding search via ChromaDB, weighted score aggregation, and basic list filtering) as agent tools. The training pipeline directly applies standard SFT and GRPO with an outcome-based accuracy/format reward without novel formulation for multi-primitive credit assignment.

Lack of latency and efficiency benchmarking: Interactive multi-turn retrieval involving dense vector search, BM25 reranking, score normalization, and multiple LLM reasoning turns introduces considerable latency and computational cost compared to standard or single-turn retrieval, yet wall-clock latency, token consumption, and compute overhead are omitted from the evaluation.

strengths: Clear conceptual motivation: The paper addresses an important bottleneck in agentic RAG where agents are typically confined to blind query reformulation against a black-box semantic retriever.

Comprehensive system design: The combination of a multi-module reasoning workflow (Global Planner, Adaptive Reasoner, Executor) for trajectory synthesis with a two-stage training paradigm (SFT + GRPO reinforcement learning) is well-thought-out and systematically implemented.

Extensive empirical evaluations: The authors evaluate across six QA benchmarks (multi-hop and single-hop) plus an out-of-domain evaluation on MultiHop-RAG, demonstrating strong performance gains against comparable baselines.

Thorough analysis and ablations: The submission includes useful ablations on individual interaction primitives, training components, retrieval efficiency (iterations vs. accuracy), and runtime computational costs.
weaknesses: Questionable evaluation corpus construction and potential data leakage: In Appendix D.3, the authors reveal that the evaluation corpus is heavily curated and downscaled to only ~280k text chunks (~21.8k documents) rather than the standard multi-million Wikipedia corpus. More concerningly, for benchmarks lacking explicit candidate evidence (e.g., Bamboogle), the authors 'generated synthetic queries from the question and ground-truth answer to retrieve the top 20 most similar passages' to populate the corpus. Augmenting the corpus using ground-truth answers risks information leakage and diverges substantially from realistic open-domain retrieval setups.

Overstated technical framing ('Dismantling the retrieval black-box'): The paper frames its approach as fundamentally peering inside and dismantling the retrieval engine, but in practice, the model is simply equipped with richer tool-calling parameters (hybrid BM25/dense search, entity filters, and chunk include/exclude lists). From the agent's perspective, this remains an API/tool-use interface rather than white-box access to retriever states or representations.

Substantial inference latency and token overhead: As shown in Table 7, Interact-RAG requires more than double the wall-clock latency (36.4s vs. 17.2s) and almost four times the generated tokens (713 vs. 192 tokens) compared to Search-R1. This makes the system considerably more expensive to deploy in practical applications.

Incomplete baseline parity and reporting artifacts: In Table 1, several key baselines in the Qwen3-8B section (Search-R1, R-Search, S-DeepSearcher) rely on 7B checkpoints due to lack of open 8B versions, which tilts the main comparison in favor of Interact-RAG. Additionally, there is an unresolved LaTeX citation/table reference ('Table ??' on page 6), reflecting minor presentation carelessness.

strengths: Compelling motivation: The paper addresses a clear and practical limitation in current agentic RAG frameworks, where agents are restricted to black-box query reformulation and frequently fall into unhelpful trial-and-error query loops.

Well-designed Corpus Interaction Engine: Exposing modular retrieval primitives (multi-faceted semantic/exact search, entity anchoring, and context shaping/document filtering) directly as tool actions gives the agent fine-grained control over information gathering.

Comprehensive system architecture: The proposed framework neatly connects a multi-module reasoning workflow (Global-Planner, Adaptive-Reasoner, Executor) used for both zero-shot reasoning and trajectory synthesis, followed by SFT and RL (GRPO) to produce an autonomous, unified end-to-end agent.

Extensive experimental validation and analyses: The empirical evaluation covers six standard benchmarks, out-of-distribution domains (MultiHop-RAG), detailed ablation studies on primitives and training stages, action frequency dynamics across training, and computational cost/latency trade-offs.
weaknesses: Potentially overstated baseline comparison: In Table 1 (bottom block for Qwen3-8B), the training-based baselines (Search-R1, R-Search, S-DeepSearcher) are evaluated using their official Qwen2.5-7B checkpoints. The claimed +9.7 EM / 22.5% relative improvement in the text heavily benefits from comparing an 8B model against 7B baselines. When comparing strictly on the Qwen2.5-7B backbone (Table 1 top block), Interact-RAG achieves 47.5 EM vs. 43.1 EM for Search-R1 (+4.4 EM, ~10% relative gain). The text should be more upfront and avoid highlighting the cross-backbone comparison as the primary headline figure.

Corpus construction and evaluation fidelity: In Appendix D.3, the evaluation corpus is curated to ~280,000 text chunks, including generating synthetic queries from questions and ground-truth answers to populate candidate passages for datasets like Bamboogle. Subsampling and pruning the search space substantially differs from standard open-corpus retrieval settings (e.g., full 2018/2020 Wikipedia with ~21M passages), potentially softening the challenge of distractor retrieval.

Novelty of the primitives: Dense retrieval, BM25 keyword search, hybrid score fusion, and entity filtering are well-established IR methods. While integrating them into an agent's toolset and policy learning is practical and well-executed, the conceptual IR primitives themselves are standard.
Presentation issue: There is an uncompiled reference on page 6 ('with the main results in Table ??').

strengths: Well-motivated concept: Transitioning RAG agents from passive, single-query issuers into active manipulators of retrieval operations (exact search, entity anchoring, score fusion, and context shaping) directly targets known failure modes of black-box dense retrieval.

Well-structured framework: The proposed progression from a modular data synthesis workflow (Global-Planner, Adaptive-Reasoner, Executor) to two-stage end-to-end training (SFT on filtered successful traces followed by GRPO reinforcement learning) is logically sound and practically effective.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The method is tested across six standard QA benchmarks (NQ, PopQA, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue, Bamboogle) and an out-of-domain benchmark (MultiHop-RAG), consistently showing clear improvements over relevant baselines including Search-R1, MA-RAG, and Search-o1.

Thorough analysis and ablations: The manuscript includes informative ablations on individual interaction primitives, training stages (SFT vs. RL), retrieval coverage, action iteration efficiency, and computational latency.
weaknesses: Corpus construction and evaluation scale: The evaluation is conducted on a downscaled, curated corpus of ~280k chunks rather than the standard open-domain full Wikipedia dump (e.g., KILT / DPR 21M passages). Furthermore, Appendix D.3 mentions using synthetic queries constructed from question and ground-truth answers to populate the corpus for some benchmarks, which could introduce bias or limit comparability to standard full-scale retrieval benchmarks.

Fairness in main model comparisons: In Table 1, for the Qwen3-8B section, key competitive baselines (Search-R1, R-Search, S-DeepSearch) are kept at 7B checkpoints due to availability, while Interact-RAG uses the 8B model. While the top half of Table 1 reports 7B results, the 8B comparison should be interpreted with caution.

Test-time latency and compute overhead: As shown in Table 7, Interact-RAG requires significantly more inference compute (36.4s latency and 713 output tokens per question compared to 17.2s and 192 tokens for Search-R1-7B), representing a substantial test-time efficiency trade-off.
Minor presentation errors: There is an unresolved LaTeX reference on page 6 ('Table ??') and a typo in Figure 2 ('Interaction Engiene').
